A [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with four [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} digits, one [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, and one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit can match the time represented by any [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet, because the product of the bases of its digits is evenly divisible by the number of [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"} in a day: 10000 &times; 9 &times; 24 &div; 86400 = 216000 &div; 86400 = 25. For [hod](#hod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"}, one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit is sufficient. The [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet selected by the range inputs below corresponds to [Hod](#hod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour of day"} \${b24hodHsl} and [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} \${hmsTodHsl}\${hmsSecHsl}\${hmsSidHsl}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: hmsinput
//| class: slider
viewof hmsinput = Inputs.form([
  Inputs.range([0, 23], {label: "Hour", value: 11, step: 1}),
  Inputs.range([0, 59], {label: "Minute", value: 0, step: 1}),
  Inputs.range([0, 59], {label: "Second", value: 0, step: 1}),
])
```

In @tbl-time below, the [quotidie]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="per day"} ([q](#q){#quotidie .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="quotidie"}) column shows how many multiples of the unit in each row can fit into one day and the [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} column uses endings called Dec terminators to transform the fraction of a day that each unit represents from a repeating decimal into a [terminating decimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeating_decimal#:~:text=a%20finite%20number%20of%20nonzero%20digits). The [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} digit in the terminators in @tbl-time represents 6 [decaseconds]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tens of seconds"} ([Ds](#decasec){#decasecond .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tens of seconds"}): 6 &div; 9 = 0.[♄]{.color6by9 .mono}.

::: {#tbl-time .unittable .overflowtable}
| Time units                                                                | [q](#q){.bold .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="per day"} | [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hour)                                | [24]{.mono}                                                             | [41.[♄]{.color6by9}]{.mono}                                       |
| [minute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute)                            | [1440]{.mono}                                                           | [&nbsp;0.[♄]{.color6by9}[η]{.color6by24}]{.mono}                  |
| [sis](#sis){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="SI seconds"}    | [86400]{.mono}                                                          | [&nbsp;0.0[☿]{.color1by9}[β]{.color1by24}]{.mono}                 |
| [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}       | [90000]{.mono}                                                          | [&nbsp;0.0[☿]{.color1by9}]{.mono}                                 |
:::

# Coordinated Universal Time {#sec-utc .hiddenheading}

Rather than use a terminator as in @tbl-time, Dec expresses one hour in [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"} as a single [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit: 0.41[♄]{.color6by9 .mono} = [β]{.color1by24 .mono}. If we add [β]{.color1by24 .mono} [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciday"} to the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, we get the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} associated with the [UTC+1 offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%2B01:00#:~:text=a%20time%20offset%20from%20UTC%20of%20%2B01%3A00): 0.\${zeroTpadHsl()} + [β]{.color1by24 .mono} &div; 10 = 0.\${utc1tintHsl()}. Currently, the Zone [0]{.color0} Dec time is \${zeroTpadHsl()}&minus;[0]{.color0} and the UTC+1 Dec time is \${utc1tpadHsl()}&minus;[β]{.color1by24 .mono}. Dec times consist of a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, a minus sign (&minus;), and an offset.

There are 12 [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets that become a terminating decimals after being converted from hours to days and therefore could be displayed in either [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} or [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"}. Although it has only ten time zones, Dec can express any [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offset using one or two non-negative [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. There are 27 [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets that require only one [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digit and 11 that need two [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits.

Out of the [38](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_UTC_offsets) [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets, 14 are negative (&lt;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}) and 24 are non-negative (&ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"}). The [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone with [the most negative offset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9212:00#:~:text=a%20nautical%20time%20zone%20comprising%20the%20high%20seas%20between%20180%C2%B0%20and%20172%C2%B030%E2%80%B2W%20longitude) is completely uninhabited. The bar chart below visualizes the population of each [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zone based on 2020 [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) data. The vast majority of all people live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with &ge;[UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets.

{{< include /dec/time/_tzpopplot.qmd >}}

Negative [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offsets only exist in [the Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas#:~:text=a%20landmass%20comprising%20the%20totality%20of%20North%20America%20and%20South%20America) and islands in the [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Atlantic_Ocean) and [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean) Oceans. Therefore, the bar chart above is essentially comparing the populations of the Americas and the rest of the world. According to 2021 [United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Department_of_Economic_and_Social_Affairs#:~:text=part%20of%20the%20United%20Nations%20Secretariat) data, roughly 1 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Americas.

Dec forbids the association of dates with negative offsets. Therefore, Dec will add ten [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} to any negative offset and add one day to the date associated with that offset. Negative offset handling has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} or the conversion of an [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet to a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and is typically only necessary after a "year month day" ([ymd](#ymd){#yearmonthday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"}) triplet is converted into a Dec date.

If we do know whether Day [364]{.color364by365} belongs to a common or leap year, adding one day to it yields either Day [0]{.color0} or Day [365]{.color365by366} and this uncertainty is expressed as a [multiplication sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplication_sign) over the last digit of [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0}. The sign hints that [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is short for [365]{.color0}&times;`leap`, where [36[5]{.acutegrave}]{.color0} is either [365]{.color365by366} if `leap` is 1 or [0]{.color0} if `leap` is 0. We can find `leap` by passing any year ([y](#y){#year .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year"}) to @eq-leap below.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup07}
$$
\text{leap}=\begin{cases}
  1&{\begin{aligned}
    &\text{ if } (\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}}} \ \ \ \ 4=0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_conjunction}{\land}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}}} 100\neq0\\
    &\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction}{\lor}(\text{y} + 1)\href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulo#:~:text=returns%20the%20remainder%20or%20signed%20remainder%20of%20a%20division}{\mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}}} 400=0\end{aligned}}\\\\
  0&{\text{ otherwise}}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-leap}

:::

# Day of week (dow) {#sec-dow .hiddenheading}

Adding one day to the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} has no effect on the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, but it increments the [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of month"} and "day of week" ([dow](#dow){#dayofweek .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of week"}). Dec meets the expectations of [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar#:~:text=the%20calendar%20currently%20used%20in%20most%20parts%20of%20the%20world) users who live in [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} time zones with negative offsets by essentially deriving the previous [dom](#dom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of month"} or [dow](#dow){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of week"} from the current [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} if a location in the Americas is provided without an offset or with a negative offset.

# Time zone offset (tzo) {#sec-tzo .hiddenheading}

In Dec, "time zone offsets" ([tzo](#tzo){#timezoneoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}) are derived solely from longitude. Dec measures [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude#:~:text=denoted%20by%20the%20Greek%20letter%20lambda) in [wěi](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E7%B7%AF#:~:text=(geography)-,latitude,-coordinate%20terms%C2%A0%E2%96%B2) ([w](#w){#wei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"}), arcbeats ([a](#a){#arcbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}), or submultiples thereof. If we travel East or West until we reach our starting point, we will cover 1 [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal line on a map"} or 100000 ([10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}) [a](#a){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="arcbeats"}. A [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} is essentially a [deciwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenth of a wěi"} ([dw](#dw){#deciwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}) longitude that became a single-digit [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"} integer via  [truncation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truncation#Truncation_and_floor_function:~:text=truncation%20is%20limiting%20the%20number%20of%20digits%20right%20of%20the%20decimal%20point) or [flooring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_and_ceiling_functions#:~:text=takes%20as%20input%20a%20real%20number%20x%2C%20and%20gives%20as%20output%20the%20greatest%20integer%20less%20than%20or%20equal%20to%20x): &LeftFloor;\${longInputHsl} &div; 100&RightFloor; = \${longFloorHsl}.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput
//| class: slider
viewof lonInput = Inputs.range([0, 999], {label: "Milliwěi", value: 500, step: 1})
```

The [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator#:~:text=the%20circle%20of%20latitude%20that%20divides%20Earth%20into%20the%20Northern%20and%20Southern%20Hemispheres) is approximately ([~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}) 1 [taur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="circumference = 𝜏r"} ([c](#c){#taur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="taur"}) or [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"} [kilozem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"} ([kz](#kz){#kilozem .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousands of zone equatorial meters"}) long. Near the Equator, a longitude that has a [precision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_degrees#Precision) of 0.1 [microwěi]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of wěi"} ([&micro;w](#uw){#microwei .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microwěi"}) or 10 milliarcbeats ([ma](#ma){#milliarcbeats .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}) is accurate to within [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}0.1 [microtaur]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millionths of taur"} ([&micro;c](#uc){#microtaur .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="microtaur"}), [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}10 "zone equatorial meters" ([zem]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="zone equatorial meters"}), or 4 [meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre#Definition:~:text=the%20base%20unit%20of%20length%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units), which is about the width of a [U-shaped living room layout](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/living-room-layouts) or the length of a typical [subcompact car](https://www.dimensions.com/collection/subcompact-cars-b-segment).

For precise [geopositioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geopositioning#:~:text=estimating%20the%20geographic%20position%20of%20an%20object%20or%20a%20person), we may want to express [geographic coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude) in [ma](#ma){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliarcbeats"}, but we are unlikely to need [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} when displaying the [solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#:~:text=a%20calculation%20of%20the%20passage%20of%20time%20based%20on%20the%20position%20of%20the%20Sun%20in%20the%20sky) or estimates of what the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} will be when the Sun rises, reaches its [highest point of the day](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon), or sets. By default, Dec uses [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} precision to display a solar time and the "solar time offset" ([sto](#sto){#solartimeoffset .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}) used to produce it.

# Solar time offset (sto) {#sec-sto .hiddenheading}

In Dec, any offset can be called a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} or a [uto](#uto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="universal time offset"}, because there will always be a longitude at which the sum of the given offset and the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} will yield solar time or [UT](#ut){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Universal Time"}. In contrast, Dec has only ten [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"}, one for each of its ten time zones. Dec translates [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} to Zone [0]{.color0} and UTC&minus;12 or UTC+12 to Zone [5]{.color5}, but does not categorize any other UTC offset as a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"}.

Dec permits any non-negative offset that is less than one day and can be written with a finite number of [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"}, [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}, and [b24](#b24){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base24"} digits. When a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} or an offset does not have a decimal separator, its measurement unit is a submultiple of a day equal to 10^-[til](#til){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time integer length"}^ days, where [til](#til){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time integer length"} is its "time integer length", its [level of precision](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_(numbers)#:~:text=level%20of%20exactness%20in%20a%20number%27s%20digits), or its digit count including any [leading zeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leading_zero#:~:text=any%200%20digit%20that%20comes%20before%20the%20first%20nonzero%20digit).

[Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm#:~:text=the%20capital%20and%20most%20populous%20city%20of%20Sweden), the capital city of [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden#:~:text=a%20Nordic%20country%20located%20on%20the%20Scandinavian%20Peninsula%20in%20Northern%20Europe)🇸🇪, is located at [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}[1]{.color1} [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"}, almost exactly on the border between Zones [0]{.color0} and [1]{.color1}. A longitude of [1]{.color1} [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"} corresponds to a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} of [05]{.color05}. The [til](#til){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time integer length"} of [05]{.color05} is 2 and therefore its measurement unit is the centiday ([cd](#cd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}), which is 10^-2^ days. We can use a multiplicative [conversion factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_of_units#:~:text=changes%20the%20unit%20without%20changing%20the%20quantity) of 10^-2^ to convert [cd](#cd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"} to [d](#d){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}: 5 &times; 10^-2^ = 0.[05]{.color05}.

Dec uses [currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency#:~:text=a%20standardized%20form%20of%20money%20used%20as%20a%20medium%20of%20exchange) names for [dd](#dd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decidays"}: [dimes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dime#Coins:~:text=coin%29%2C%20a-,ten%2Dcent%20coin,-and%20subunit%20of), [cd](#cd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}: [cents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent#Currency:~:text=a%20one%2Dhundredth%20subdivision%20of%20several%20units%20of%20currency) (&cent;), and [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"}: [mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_(currency)#:~:text=a%20subunit%20of%20currency%2C%20used%20in%20several%20countries%20as%201%E2%81%841000%20of%20the%20base%20unit) (₥). Drawing inspiration from music and writing, Dec refers to [dmd](#dmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="decimilliday"} as "lines" ([l]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="lines"}) and [cmd](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} as "beats" ([b]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beats"}). In [poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry#:~:text=a%20form%20of%20literary%20art%20that%20uses%20aesthetic%20and%20often%20rhythmic%5B1%5D%5B2%5D%5B3%5D%20qualities%20of%20language%20to%20evoke%20meanings) and [playwriting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playwright#:~:text=For%20the%20ancient%20Greeks%2C%20playwriting%20involved%20po%C3%AFesis%2C%20%22the%20act%20of%20making%22.%20This%20is%20the%20source%20of%20the%20English%20word%20poet.), notably the [works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_works_by_William_Shakespeare#:~:text=39%20plays%20and%20154%20sonnets) of [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare#:~:text=an%20English%20playwright%2C%20poet%20and%20actor), [decasyllable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decasyllable#:~:text=a%20poetic%20meter%20of%20ten%20syllables) and [iambic pentameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iambic_pentameter#:~:text=the%20rhythm%2C%20or%20meter%2C%20established%20by%20the%20words%20in%20each%20line) mandate ten [syllables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable#:~:text=a%20basic%20unit%20of%20organization%20within%20a%20sequence%20of%20speech%20sounds) per [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_%28poetry%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20writing%20into%20which%20a%20poem%20or%20play%20is%20divided%3A%20literally%2C%20a%20single%20row%20of%20text). In music, [line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line#Terminology_2:~:text=a%20strand%20or%20melody%20of%20music%20played%20by%20an%20individual%20instrument%20or%20voice), [melody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody#:~:text=a%20linear%20succession%20of%20musical%20tones%20that%20the%20listener%20perceives%20as%20a%20single%20entity), [part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Part_%28music%29#:~:text=a%20component%20of%20a%20musical%20composition), and [tune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music#Tune:~:text=a%20short%20instrumental%20piece) are synonyms. 

::: {.callout-warning}
# Bad Pun Alert
It took me forever and a **deciday** to come up with a pun for Declock⏰. I kept **second**-guessing myself and got really **wound** up, so I decided to take a **beat**. Then, I **zoned** out until it finally **struck** me: it's about **time**!
:::

# Mean solar time {#sec-mst .hiddenheading}

Outside of Dec, longitudes are often provided in [Greenwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_meridian_&28Greenwich&29#:~:text=a%20geographical%20reference%20line%20that%20passes%20through%20the%20Royal%20Observatory%2C%20Greenwich%2C%20in%20London%2C%20England) [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20measurement%20of%20a%20plane%20angle%20in%20which%20one%20full%20rotation%20is%20assigned%20the%20value%20of%20360%20degrees) ([g°](#gdeg){#greenwichdegrees .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Greenwich degrees"}). @eq-deg2wei converts [g°](#gdeg){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Greenwich degrees"} to [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="wěi"} and @eq-wei2deg does the opposite. To obtain a [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"}, we can pass [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="wěi"} to @eq-wei2sto or [g°](#gdeg){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Greenwich degrees"} to @eq-deg2sto below. As shown in @eq-mst below, we can sum an [sto](#sto){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar time offset"} with the Zone [0]{.color0} [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} to get a yearly average of solar time called "[mean solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Mean_solar_time:~:text=it%20follows%20an%20imaginary%20%22mean%20Sun%22%20that%20moves%20along%20the%20celestial%20equator%20at%20a%20constant%20rate%20that%20matches%20the%20real%20Sun%27s%20average%20rate%20over%20the%20year)" ([mst](#mst){#meansolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"}).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup08}
$$\text{w} = (\text{g}^\circ + 378) \div 360 \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-deg2wei}

$$\text{g}^\circ = (\text{w} + 0.45) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 360 - 180$$ {#eq-wei2deg}

$$\text{sto} = (0.95 + \text{w}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-wei2sto}

$$\text{sto} = (\text{g}^\circ + 360) \div 360 \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-deg2sto}

$$\text{mst} = (\text{tod} + \text{sto}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-mst}
:::

# Equation of time (eot) {#sec-eot .hiddenheading}

If we want to tailor our solar time calculations to a specific [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} instead of an average for the entire year, we can calculate "[apparent solar time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_time#Apparent_solar_time:~:text=the%20apparent%20motion%20of%20the%20actual%20Sun)" ([ast](#ast){#apparentsolartime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}) by summing [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} with the "[equation of time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equation_of_time#:~:text=the%20discrepancy%20between%20two%20kinds%20of%20solar%20time)" ([eot](#eot){#equationoftime .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"}), as shown in @eq-ast.
Obtaining the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} requires a "time of year" ([toy](#toy){#timeofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}), which is an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} that was converted from days to years as displayed in @eq-toy.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup09}
$$\text{ast} = (0.95 + \text{tod} + \text{w} +  \text{eot}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-ast}

$$\text{toy} = \text{ada} \div \text{syl}$$ {#eq-toy}

$$\text{syl} = \text{leap} + 365$$ {#eq-syl}
:::

To obtain a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"}, we divide an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} by a "solar year length" ([syl](#syl){#solaryearlength .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar year length"}), which is the number of days in the year. Dec passes the [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} directly from @eq-toy to the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} function in @eq-eot without first multiplying it by 2𝜋 or 𝜏 to convert it from [turns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_%28angle%29#:~:text=a%20unit%20of%20plane%20angle%20measurement%20equal%20to%202%CF%80%C2%A0radians%2C%20360%C2%A0degrees) ([t](#t){#turn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}) to [radians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radian#:~:text=the%20unit%20of%20angle%20in%20the%20International%20System%20of%20Units) ([rad](#rad){#radian .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}) because the [sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20side%20opposite%20that%20angle%20to%20the%20length%20of%20the%20longest%20side%20of%20the%20triangle) and [cos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=the%20ratio%20of%20the%20length%20of%20the%20adjacent%20leg%20to%20that%20of%20the%20hypotenuse) [trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions#:~:text=functions%20which%20relate%20an%20angle%20of%20a%20right%2Dangled%20triangle%20to%20ratios%20of%20two%20side%20lengths) used by Dec are designed for [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} instead of [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup10}
$$\begin{split}
\text{eot} & = \beta_0 \\
& + \beta_1 \times \text{cos(toy)} \\
& + \beta_2 \times \text{sin(toy)} \\
& + \beta_3 \times \text{cos(2} \times \text{toy)} \\
& + \beta_4 \times \text{sin(2} \times \text{toy)}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-eot}
:::

By comparing the `sincost` and `sincos` functions, the code below demonstrates that using [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} rather than [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} can [yield more accurate results](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_and_cosine#:~:text=Representing%20angles%20in%20turns%20or%20half%2Dturns%20has%20accuracy%20advantages). Whereas `sincost` expects to receive [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} and is always correct, `sincos` assumes that it will get [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"} and generates the slightly incorrect [E notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_notation#E_notation) values below because it cannot produce zero unless its input is zero.

:::{.panel-tabset group="language"}
### Julia

```{julia}
sincost(x) = sincospi(2 * x)
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### Observable JavaScript

```{ojs}
sincospi = require(
  'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/stdlib-js/math-base-special-sincospi@umd/browser.js'
  )
function sincost(x) {
  return sincospi(2 * x);
}
function sincos(x) {
  return [Math.sin(x), Math.cos(x)]
}
sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * Math.PI)
sincos(1 * 2 * Math.PI)
```

### Python

```{python}
from math import cos, sin, pi, cospi, sinpi

def sincost(x):
    x *= 2
    return sinpi(x), cospi(x)

def sincos(x):
    return sin(x), cos(x)

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

### R

```{r}
sincost <- function(x) {
  x <- 2 * x
  c(sinpi(x), cospi(x))
}

sincos <- function(x) {
  c(sin(x), cos(x))
}

sincost(0.25)
sincost(0.5)
sincost(0.75)
sincost(1)
sincos(0.25 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.5 * 2 * pi)
sincos(0.75 * 2 * pi)
sincos(1 * 2 * pi)
```

:::

The values below are the coefficients of a [harmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic#:~:text=positive%20integer%20multiple%20of%20the%20fundamental%20frequency) [model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_model#:~:text=embodies%20a%20set%20of%20statistical%20assumptions%20concerning%20the%20generation%20of%20sample%20data), adapted from the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.noaa.gov) ([NOAA](#noaa){#nationaloceanicandatmosphericadministration .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"}) [General Solar Position Calculations](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/solareqns.PDF). Before [fitting](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.optimize.curve_fit.html) the model to [NOAA](#noaa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration"} [yearly solar data](https://gml.noaa.gov/grad/solcalc/calcdetails.html), Dec divides [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values by 1.44 to convert minutes to [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"}, converts [ymd](#ymd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year month day"} triplet dates and [hms](#hms){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hour minute second"} triplet times into [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregates"}, and sorts by [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}.

{{< embed eot.ipynb#eotcoef >}}

{{< include /dec/time/_eotplot.qmd >}}

In the [line📈chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_chart#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20chart%20that%20displays%20information%20as%20a%20series%20of%20data%20points%20called%20%27markers%27%20connected%20by%20straight%20line%20segments) above, the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values range from -9.8 to 11.4 [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="millidays"} and the range of [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"}, [-365]{.color0} to [365]{.color365by366}, represents a common year followed by a leap year. The [absolute value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_value#:~:text=non%2Dnegative%29-,magnitude%20of,measured%20without%20regard%20to%20its%20sign,-.%20Namely%2C) of the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} reaches about one [centiday]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="hundredth of a day"} ([cd]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centiday"}) on Days [245]{.color245by365} and [349]{.color349by365}, but passes through zero on Days [45]{.color045by365}, [103]{.color103by365}, [184]{.color184by365}, and [299]{.color299by365}. Therefore, [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} are equivalent four times per year.

Apart from transforming an [mst](#mst){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="mean solar time"} into an [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, we can also use [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} values to more accurately estimate the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} of [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow), sunrise, and sunset. @eq-solarnoon below creates a [solar noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon#:~:text=reaching%20its%20highest%20position%20above%20the%20horizon%20on%20that%20day%20and%20casting%20the%20shortest%20shadow) [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} by keeping only the decimal part of the result of subtracting a [w](#w){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="horizontal lines on a map"} longitude and an [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} value that is measured in days from the sum of 9.55 and a [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offset"} that is measured in days.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup11}
$$\text{solarnoon} = \left(9.55 + \text{tzo} - \text{w} - \text{eot}\right) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1$$ {#eq-solarnoon}
:::

# Cambridge and Cambridge {#sec-cac .hiddenheading}

To compare the solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} in two cities, we can plug the longitude of each city into @eq-solarnoon above. If all of the variables other than longitude in @eq-solarnoon are set to zero, the resulting solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is almost five [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge#:~:text=a%20city%20and%20non%2Dmetropolitan%20district%20in%20the%20county%20of%20Cambridgeshire%2C%20England) in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom#:~:text=a%20country%20in%20Northwestern%20Europe) and nearly seven [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} for [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts#:~:text=a%20city%20in%20Middlesex%20County%2C%20Massachusetts%2C%20United%20States) in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States#:~:text=a%20country%20primarily%20located%20in%20North%20America).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup12}
$$4.99635 = (9.55 - 0.050365) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk}

$$6.97517 = (9.55 - 0.852484) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema}
:::

The two homonymous cities are about two [dw](#dw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="deciwěi"} apart and therefore will always differ by around two [decidays]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="tenths of a day"} in solar time, regardless of what time zone we use as our frame of reference. England is in Zone [0]{.color0} and Massachusetts is in Zone [8]{.color8}. From the perspective of Zone [8]{.color8}, solar noon is roughly [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [5]{.color5} in Cambridge, MA and about [Tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} [3]{.color3} in Cambridge, UK.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup13}
$$2.99635 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.050365) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgeuk8}

$$4.97517 = (9.55 + 0.8 - 0.852484) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 \times 10$$ {#eq-cambridgema8}
:::

# Light arc whole (law) {#sec-law .hiddenheading}

The path in the sky that the Sun appears to follow from a sunrise to a sunset is a "light [arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_path#:~:text=arc%2Dlike%20path%20that%20the%20Sun%20appears%20to%20follow%20across%20the%20sky) whole" ([law](#law){#lightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}). Solar noon, the midpoint of a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}, is halfway between sunrise and sunset. A [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} can be evenly split into two "light arc halves" ([lah](#lah){#lightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"}). Whereas [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} are time points, [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc wholes"} and [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc halves"} are durations. The difference between a solar noon [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} is a sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup14}
$$\text{law} = \text{lah} \times 2$$ {#eq-law}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunrise}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} \\
& = \text{sunset} - \text{law}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunrise}

$$\begin{split}
\text{sunset}
& = \text{solarmidnight} + \text{nah} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{sunrise} + \text{law} \\
& = \text{solarnoon} + \text{lah} \\
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sunset}
:::

## Night arc whole (naw) {#sec-naw .unnumbered .hiddenheading}

The Sun continues its path after it disappears below the horizon, moving from sunset to sunrise along a "night arc whole" ([naw](#naw){#nightarcwhole .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"}). Like [conjugate angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=conjugate%20angles%20sum%20to%20a%20full%20angle), a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} form a full circle that represents one day. Likewise, a [lah](#lah){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc half"} and a "night arc half" ([nah](#nah){#nightarchalf .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc half"}) are like two [supplementary angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle#:~:text=sum%20to%20a%20straight%20angle) that form a semicircle from solar noon to the [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} midpoint: [solar midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight#:~:text=the%20time%20opposite%20to%20solar%20noon%2C%20when%20the%20Sun%20is%20closest%20to%20the%20nadir%2C%20and%20the%20night%20is%20equidistant%20from%20dusk%20and%20dawn).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup15}
$$\text{naw} = \text{nah} \times 2$$ {#eq-naw}

$$\begin{split}
\text{day}
& = \text{law} + \text{naw} \\
& = (\text{lah} + \text{nah}) \times 2
\end{split}$$ {#eq-day}

$$\begin{split}
\text{solarmidnight}
&= \text{sunrise} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{solarnoon} - \text{lah} - \text{nah} \\
&= \text{sunset} - \text{law} - \text{nah}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-solarmidnight}
:::

The range input below controls the yellow [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} and the blue [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} in the diagram beneath it. At the Equator, the sun always rises about a quarter turn from North and sets around three quarter turns from North, resulting in a [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of roughly half a day: 75% &minus; 25% = 50%. If the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is zero, a [polar night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_night#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20below%20the%20horizon%20for%20more%20than%2024%C2%A0hours) occurs. A day without a [naw](#naw){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="night arc whole"} is called a [polar day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight_sun#:~:text=the%20Sun%20remains%20visible%20at%20the%20local%20midnight).

{{< include /dec/time/_dayarcplot.qmd >}}

# Solar azimuth angle (saa) {#sec-saa .hiddenheading}

The numbers in the diagram above are "[solar azimuth angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_azimuth_angle#:~:text=horizontal%20angle%20with%20respect%20to%20north)" ([saa](#saa){#solarazimuthangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) [milliturns]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="thousandths of a turn"} ([mt](#mt){#milliturn .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}). At solar noon, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} is 0 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20%28hemisphere%29%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20south%20of%20the%20equator) and 500 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"} in the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere#:~:text=the%20half%20of%20Earth%20that%20is%20north%20of%20the%20equator). The [radio](https://observablehq.github.io/framework/inputs/radio#:~:text=allows%20the%20user%20to%20choose%20one%20of%20a%20given%20set%20of%20values)📻input above controls whether the midpoint of the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is 0 or 500 [mt](#mt){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliturns"}. To measure the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} during the [daytime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daytime#:~:text=the%20period%20of%20the%20day%20in%20which%20the%20Sun%20is%20above%20the%20local%20horizon%20in%20a%20given%20location), point a compass🧭at the spot on the horizon below the Sun.

# Solar elevation angle (sea) {#sec-sea .hiddenheading}

During an [equinox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator) at the Equator, the Sun goes from East to West directly overhead, the [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} flips like a switch from 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} to 0.75 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} at solar noon, the "[solar elevation angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_zenith_angle#Summary_of_special_angles:~:text=For%20example%2C%20the-,solar,-elevation%20angle%20is)" ([sea](#sea){#solarelevationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}) peaks at 0.25 [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"}, and [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} is 0.5 &minus; sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}) &times; (0.25 &minus; [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}). To obtain the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, we can use the height (h) of a vertical rod on a level surface and the length (L) of its shadow: [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"} = atan2(h, L).

# Inverse trigonometric functions {#sec-itf .hiddenheading}

In addition to determining the [sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}, the  [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) function can also be used to calculate [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"}, as shown in @eq-astjing, where [j](#j){#jing .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} is a latitude measured in turns called [jīng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_arc#Full_meridian_(polar_perimeter):~:text=The%20polar%20Earth%27s%20circumference%20is%20simply%20four%20times%20quarter%20meridian) ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"}). In Dec, [inverse trigonometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions#:~:text=obtain%20an%20angle%20from%20any%20of%20the%20angle%27s%20trigonometric%20ratios) functions like [atan2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2#:~:text=function%20atan2%20is-,the%202%2Dargument%20arctangent,-.%20By%20definition%2C) yield [t](#t){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="turns"} as opposed to [rad](#rad){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="radians"}. At the Equator ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0), the latitude is zero and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 + atan2(-sin([saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"})cos([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"}), sin([sea](#sea){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar elevation angle"})).

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup16}
$$
\text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{atan2}\!\!\left(
\begin{aligned}
& \text{-sin(saa)cos(sea),} \\
& \text{sin(sea)cos(j) } - \\
& \text{cos(saa)cos(sea)sin(j)}
\end{aligned}
\right)
$$ {#eq-astjing}

$$
\text{ast} =
\begin{cases}
\text{saa} & \text{j} = 0.25 \\
\text{atan2(-sin(saa)cos(sea), sin(sea))} & \text{j} = 0 \\
(1.5 - \text{saa}) \mathbin{-\mkern-3.5mu\raise{0.073em}{\scriptstyle\lfloor}} 1 & \text{j} = -0.25
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-extremes}
:::

At the North Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = 0.25), the latitude is 0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"}. At the South Pole ([j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} = -0.25), the latitude is -0.25 [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} and @eq-astjing simplifies to [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 0.5 &minus; [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} before solar noon or [ast](#ast){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="apparent solar time"} = 1.5 &minus; [saa](#saa){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar azimuth angle"} after solar noon. In between the Equator and the South or North Pole (-0.25 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0 &or; 0 < [j](#j){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="jīng"} < 0.25), we should use Equation -@eq-ast, -@eq-astjing, or -@eq-astsha.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup17}
$$
\text{ast} = 0.5 + \text{arccos}\!\!\left(\dfrac{\text{sin(sea)} - \text{sin(j)sin(sda)}}{\text{cos(j)cos(sda)}}\right) \times
\begin{cases}
\text{-}1 & 0 \le \text{saa} < 0.5 \\
1 & 0.5 \le \text{saa} < 1
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-astsha}
:::

# Solar declination angle {#sec-sda .hiddenheading}

Unlike @eq-astjing, @eq-astsha requires a "solar declination angle" ([sda](#sda){#solardeclinationangle .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}). Whereas latitude is the angle from the Equator in the [geographic coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20spherical%20or%20geodetic%20coordinate%20system%20for%20measuring%20and%20communicating%20positions%20directly%20on%20Earth%20as%20latitude%20and%20longitude), [declination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declination#:~:text=the%20angular%20distance%20from%20the%20celestial%20equator%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere) is the angle from the [celestial equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_equator) in the [equatorial coordinate system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_coordinate_system#:~:text=a%20celestial%20coordinate%20system%20widely%20used%20to%20specify%20the%20positions%20of%20celestial%20objects). For simplicity, we can use @eq-eot for both the [eot](#eot){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="equation of time"} and [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"}. The line plot below shows [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angles"} over the course of a year.

{{< include /dec/time/_sdaplot.qmd >}}

In the line plot above, [zero crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_crossing#:~:text=a%20point%20where%20the%20sign%20of%20a%20mathematical%20function%20changes) are [equinoxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox#:~:text=a%20moment%20in%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20appears%20directly%20above%20the%20equator%2C%20rather%20than%20to%20its%20north%20or%20south) and [stationary points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stationary_point#:~:text=a%20point%20on%20the%20graph%20of%20the%20function%20where%20the%20function%27s%20derivative%20is%20zero) are [solstices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solstice#:~:text=the%20time%20when%20the%20Sun%20reaches%20its%20most%20northerly%20or%20southerly%20sun%20path%20relative%20to%20the%20celestial%20equator%20on%20the%20celestial%20sphere). From the northward to the southward equinox, the [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} is positive and every [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} in the Northern Hemisphere is longer than the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} at the Equator, which is longer than every [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} in the Southern Hemisphere. The opposite is true from the southward to the northward equinox.

The chart below splits the [Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/centers/sedac-daac) population data into two bars representing the Northern and Southern Hemispheres and then further divides each bar by [UTC](#utc){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Coordinated Universal Time"} offset. Nearly 7 billion out of a total of almost 8 billion people live in the Northern Hemisphere and therefore experience the longest [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} of the year at the [northern solstice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_solstice#:~:text=In%20the%20Northern%20Hemisphere%2C%20the%20June%20solstice%20is%20the%20summer%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20longest%20period%20of%20daylight%29%2C%20while%20in%20the%20Southern%20Hemisphere%20it%20is%20the%20winter%20solstice%20%28the%20day%20with%20the%20shortest%20period%20of%20daylight%29).

{{< include /dec/time/_hemipopplot.qmd >}}

The top range input below picks the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} that we will turn into a [toy](#toy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of year"} and then pass to our [sda](#sda){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="solar declination angle"} model. The two range inputs beneath the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} input choose the geographic coordinates needed to find the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"}. While the sunrise and sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"} rely on all three range inputs, the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} depends on the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and latitude but not on longitude: \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} &minus; \${selectedSunrise.toFixed(3)} = \${parseFloat(daytimeDuration.toFixed(3))}.

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup18}
$$\text{sunset} - \text{sunrise} = \text{law}$$ {#eq-sunrise}
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: doyinput
//| class: slider
viewof doyInput = Inputs.range([0, 365], {label: "Day of year", value: 183, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: latinput
//| class: slider
viewof latInput = Inputs.range([-250, 250], {label: "Latitude", value: 0, step: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: loninput1
//| class: slider
Inputs.bind(Inputs.range([0, 1000], {label: "Longitude", value: 500, step: 1}), viewof lonInput)
```

In the equation above, the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is the [minuend](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/minuend#:~:text=A%20number%20or%20quantity%20from%20which%20another%20is%20to%20be%20subtracted), the sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} is the [subtrahend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#:~:text=number%20being%20subtracted), and the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} is the [difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtraction#Notation_and_terminology:~:text=The%20result%20is%20the%20difference): sunset &minus; sunrise = [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"}. If we replace the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the sunrise [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} with the sunset [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}, the difference will no longer be the [law](#law){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="light arc whole"} but rather the time until sunset if it is negative or since sunset if it is positive: \${selectedCurrent.toFixed(3)} = \${selectedSunset.toFixed(3)} [${selectedDifference < 0 ? "-" : "+"}]{.mono} \${parseFloat(Math.abs(selectedDifference).toFixed(3))}.

# Current elapsed remaining {#sec-cer .hiddenheading}

In general, the subtrahend is the time of an event such as a rocket🚀launch and the difference is the negative [remaining time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=the%20time%20remaining%20before%20an%20event) if the minuend is less than the subtrahend or the positive [elapsed time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Elapsed_Time) if the minuend is greater than the subtrahend. When the minuend is the current time, the difference acts as a "[T minus (T&minus;) countdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=a%20sequence%20of%20backward%20counting%20to%20indicate%20the%20time%20remaining)" or "[T plus (T+) countup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown#:~:text=After%20a%20launch%2C%20most%20countdown%20clocks%20begin%20to%20show%20Mission%20Elapsed%20Time)".

::: {.equationgroup #equationgroup19}
$$\begin{cases}\text{difference}<0&{\text{if } \text{minuend} < \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}=0&{\text{if minuend} = \text{subtrahend};}\\\text{difference}>0&{\text{if minuend}>\text{subtrahend.}}\end{cases}$$ {#eq-difference}
:::

# Positive interval tod (pit) {#sec-pit .hiddenheading}

A [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} can be either a "positive interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([pit](#pit){#positiveintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"}) that counts up the time since the "beginning of day" ([bod](#bod){#beginningofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of day"}) or a "negative interval [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"}" ([nit](#nit){#negativeintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}) that counts down the time until the "end of day" ([eod](#eod){#endofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"}). The difference between a [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} and an [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"} is a [nit](#nit){#negativeintervaltod .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}: [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} &minus; [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"} = [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}. The [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"} is equal to one day or [10^5^]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"} [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}. In [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}, the current Zone [0]{.color0} [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"} is \${zeroTintHsl()} &minus; [[10^5^]{data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}]{.color0} = \${negaTintHsl()}. 

# Positive integer doy (pid) {#sec-pid .hiddenheading}

Similarly, a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} can be either a "positive integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([pid](#pid){#positiveintegerdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"}) that counts up the days since the "beginning of year" ([boy](#boy){#beginningofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="beginning of year"}) or a "negative integer [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}" ([nid](#nid){#negativeintegerdoy .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"}) that counts down the days until the "end of year" ([eoy](#eoy){#endofyear .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"}) and an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} can be either a "positive interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([pia](#pia){#positiveintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"}) that joins a [pid](#pid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive integer day of year"} and [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} or a "negative interval [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"}" ([nia](#nia){#negativeintervalada .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"}) that links a [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} and [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}: [nia](#nia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"} = [nid](#nid){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative integer day of year"} + [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"} = [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} &minus; [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"}.

When a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} and a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} are in the same equation, we multiple the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} by a conversion factor or divide it by an inverse conversion factor so that its measurement unit matches that of the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}: \${zeroDotyHsl()}.\${zeroTpadHsl()} = \${zeroDotyHsl()} + \${zeroTintHsl()} &div; [[10^5^]{data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}]{.color0} = \${nextDotyHsl()} + \${negaTintHsl()} &div; [[10^5^]{data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="one hundred thousand"}]{.color0}. If the subtrahend is an [eod](#eod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of day"}, it disappears after advancing the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} by one day and turning the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} from a [pit](#pit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval tod"} into a [nit](#nit){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval tod"}.

# Year of era (yoe) {#sec-yoe .hiddenheading}

Likewise, a subtrahend that is an [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"} is not displayed as part of a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} or an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} because it becomes incorporated into the "year of era" ([yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}): \${zeroYearHsl()} + \${zeroDotyHsl()}.\${zeroTpadHsl()} &div; [\${zeroNdaysInYear}]{.color0} = \${nextYearHsl()} + \${zeroNidHsl()}.\${negaTendHsl()} &div; [\${zeroNdaysInYear}]{.color0}. Essentially, the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"} takes up any amount of time that spills over from the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"} absorbs any amount of time that does not fit into the [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="day of year"}.

The [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} is like a [sōzu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shishi-odoshi#:~:text=a%20type%20of%20water%20fountain%20used%20in%20Japanese%20gardens), a Japanese garden fountain that fills until it reaches a tipping point, empties out, and then begins to fill up again. In this analogy,  time flows like water from the [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregate"} to the [yoe](#yoe){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="year of era"}, the [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"} is the total volume of the sōzu, the [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} is the volume that is filled with water, and the absolute value of the [nia](#nia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"} is the volume that is empty: [eoy](#eoy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="end of year"} = [pia](#pia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="positive interval ada"} &minus; [nia](#nia){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="negative interval ada"}. 

::: {.column-margin fig-align="center" .gif #sozu}
![](/asset/Higashiyama_Botanical_Garden_Shishiodoshi_20170617.gif)
[[Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Higashiyama_Botanical_Garden_Shishiodoshi_20170617.gif)]{.giflabel #sozulabel}
:::

# Time of milliday (tom) {#sec-tom .hiddenheading}

Just as we can divide an [ada](#ada){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="annual day aggregates"} into a [doy](#doy){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days of year"} and [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="times of day"}, we can split a [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} into a "milliday of day" ([mod](#mod){#millidayofday .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday of day"}) and a "time of milliday" ([tom](#tom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of milliday"}): [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} = [mod](#mod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday of day"} &times; 100 + [tom](#tom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of milliday"}. Multiplying a [mod](#mod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday of day"} by 100 converts it from [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} to [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}. To distinguish the [tom](#tom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of milliday"} from the [mod]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday of day"}, we can express the first digit of the [tom](#tom){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of milliday"} in [b9](#b9){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base9"} rather than [b10](#b10){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="base10"}: \${zeroTmonHsl()}\${zeroTtopHsl()} = \${zeroTmonHsl()} &times; 100 + \${zeroTtonHsl()} &asymp; \${zeroTmonHsl()}\${decsepHsl()} = \${zeroTmonHsl()} &times; 100 + \${decsecHsl()}.

# Simulated watch face {#sec-swf .hiddenheading}

The range input below sets the [tzo](#tzo){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time zone offsets"} for the watch [face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock_face#:~:text=displays%20time%20through%20the%20use%20of%20a%20flat%20dial%20with%20reference%20marks) simulation beneath it. The radio inputs in between the range input and simulation determine whether the simulated watch face is circular or rectangular and whether it has 90 [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"} or 100 [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"} [marks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatch_mark#Unit_and_value_marks:~:text=The%20distance%20between%20adjacent%20marks%20is%20one%20unit). An [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} divides evenly into thirds, sixths, or ninths with [s](#s){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="Dec seconds"}, quarters with [cmd](#cmd){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="centimillidays"}, and halves, fifths, or tenths with either unit.

{{< include /dec/time/_watch.qmd >}}

The "Ticks" radio input above refers to the tick marks on the simulated watch face above and how many times the simulated watch ticks per [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} ([&permil;](#permil){#permilliday .mono .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="per milliday"}). I used the [`librosa`](https://librosa.org) [Python]() [library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_%28computing%29#:~:text=a%20collection%20of%20resources%20that%20can%20be%20used%20during%20software%20development) to determine that the [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo#:~:text=pace%20of%20a%20given%20composition) of the [1988]{.color88by100} song "[Don't Worry, Be Happy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don%27t_Worry,_Be_Happy#:~:text=a%201988%20song%20by%20Bobby%20McFerrin)" is [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}100.566 [&permil;](#permil){.mono .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="per milliday"} or [~]{.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="approximately"}1.00566 per [cmd](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} ([&thorn;](#per){#perbeat .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeat"}). Whereas [&permil;](#permil){.mono .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="per milliday"} and [&thorn;](#per){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="perbeat"} measure [rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_%28mathematics%29#:~:text=the%20denominator%20is%20a%20time%20duration), [md](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} and [cmd](#md){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday"} measure
[durations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duration#:~:text=amount%20of%20time%20elapsed%20between%20two%20events).

# Webpage load time {#sec-wlt .hiddenheading}

The difference in between a minuend and subtrahend is intended to be a duration, whereas the minuend and subtrahend themselves are supposed to be [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} that represent [time points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_point#:~:text=an%20instant%2C%20analogous%20to%20a%20geometrical%20point%20in%20space). If the minuend is the current [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} and the subtrahend is the [tod](#tod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="time of day"} when this webpage loaded, the difference will be the duration since this webpage loaded: \${zeroTintHsl()} = \${loadTimeHsl()} + \${elaTimeHsl()}. 

Dec is not the first system to use [decimal time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_time#France). During the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution), decimal time was mandatory for French public records for 197 days ([d](#d){#day .tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="days"}), from [1794]{.color94by100}+[205]{.color205by365} to [1795]{.color95by100}+[037]{.color037by365}. On [1998]{.color98by100}+[247]{.color247by365}, the Swatch corporation announced [Swatch Internet Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swatch_Internet_Time), which divides the day into 1000 ".beats", only has one time zone, and is displayed by Dec as [mod](#mod){.tool data-bs-toggle="tooltip" data-bs-title="milliday of day"}&minus;[&beta;]{.color1by24}.

# Next {#next .unnumbered}

The next article in the [Dec section](/dec) of my [site](/) shows how we can combine [Dec dates](/dec/date) and times into [Dec snaps](/dec/snap)🫰, which are analogous to the [combined date and time representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Combined_date_and_time_representations) in the [ISO 8601](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#:~:text=an%20international%20standard%20covering%20the%20worldwide%20exchange%20and%20communication%20of%20date%20and%20time%2Drelated%20data) international standard for dates and times. The final article in the Dec section demonstrates how Dec dates, times, and snaps🫰can be paired up to express [time intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_8601#Time_intervals:~:text=the%20intervening%20time%20between%20two%20time%20points) called Dec [spans](/dec/span)🌈.
